transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-07
Start: 10:00 AM PDT
Duration: ~63 minutes

Summary (auto): POC to validate ephemeral prompt handling and redaction across Redwood private deployment; focus on minimizing retained prompt storage, verifying redaction rules for PHI, and sizing a benchmark (~100–200 rps, 1.5M tokens/day) to prove latency and cost.

---- Transcript ----
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, with Carlos from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Dr. Lina Ortiz: Doing well, thanks. We — we've been, um, trying to consolidate our vendor POCs so appreciate you doing this.
[00:12] Carlos Nguyen: Thanks Lina. Quick run of attendees?
[00:15] Jared Kim: Jared here, privacy lead. My key aim is to make sure protected health info never lands in persistent logs and that we can prove redaction works.
[00:23] Aisha Rahman: Aisha, ML eng. I'll own the workload side and hand over sample payloads.
[00:27] Samir Desai: Samir, SRE, I'll be on infra and access.
[00:31] Maya Patel: Great. Agenda: define success criteria, agree workload sizing, discuss redaction/retention/KMS options, and align timeline — then next steps.

[00:45] Carlos Nguyen: To start: can you describe the actual prompt flows? Are you sending full clinical notes or structured fields plus instructions?
[00:52] Aisha Rahman: It's a mix. Mostly structured fields — patient demographics + op notes snippets — about 250–500 tokens per interaction, sometimes longer for summary generation. We want to avoid persisting any free-text that could have PHI.
[01:05] Carlos Nguyen: Got it. Two quick levers we typically recommend: ephemeral prompt storage where the platform holds context only in-memory and drops it after response, and field-level redaction where certain fields are hashed or removed before logging. Both are available but tradeoffs exist.
[01:20] Dr. Lina Ortiz: Lina: For compliance, we need the option for no persisted prompt storage at all for a subset of PII flows — so ephemeral only — but also an auditable proof that redactions occurred. Is that doable?
[01:30] Carlos Nguyen: Yes — a common pattern: client-side pseudonymization (hashing IDs) + ephemeral prompts in the inference plane, and then we emit a small audit record (non-PII) that says "redaction rule X applied" with a checksum. The audit record can be pushed to your SIEM. Note that checksums must avoid reversible content.
[01:48] Jared Kim: We need that checksum plus a secure KMS key separation. We don't want Redwood holding unwrapped keys. Can you support customer-managed KMS/HSM?
[01:56] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS integrations for Private deployments. For Hosted we can do envelope encryption with customer KEKs via HSM. For an on-prem or VPC deployment, keys remain in your KMS. There may be some ops work to bind the runtime.
[02:12] Samir Desai: If we go the private route we also want to validate throughput. Our baseline today is about 120 rps during business hours, spiky bursts to 300 rps for short windows.
[02:22] Maya Patel: Good, that helps sizing. For the POC we typically advise a benchmark plan: baseline run at your 120 rps steady, a spike test to 300 rps for 10 minutes, and token/day validation for ~1.5–2M tokens/day. Does that match expectations?
[02:36] Aisha Rahman: Yes that's inline. Also want to check p95 latency under 350ms for short prompts and below 700ms for the longer 1k+ token summarizations.
[02:46] Carlos Nguyen: We'll target p95 < 350ms for <512-token requests on a dedicated test pool. For longer requests latency will increase; we can show model-variant tradeoffs.
[02:58] Dr. Lina Ortiz: On redaction verification, can you walk through how we test that redaction rules are enforced end-to-end?
[03:06] Carlos Nguyen: Sure. Typical approach: we provide synthetic PHI-laden test inputs (you provide or we can synthesize) and then run two checks — 1) server-side logs where we assert no raw PHI tokens are present, and 2) output inspection to ensure expected placeholders or hashed tokens appear. We'll also run a differential test where we temporarily turn off redaction to show the difference — that's just for validation.
[03:28] Jared Kim: That differential test is useful. But we need guardrails: do not run differential on production data.
[03:33] Maya Patel: Agreed. Everything for the POC will be on a controlled sample set.
[03:37] Carlos Nguyen: On the implementation detail: our platform supports both native redaction masks (you can specify JSON path rules) and regex-based rules. For complex clinical text, we sometimes recommend an upstream preprocessor that tags PHI spans and replaces them with stable pseudonyms before hitting the inference plane.
[03:53] Aisha Rahman: Stable pseudonyms are important for continuity across interactions. If we hash patient_id with salt, we can keep referential integrity without exposing identity.
[04:01] Carlos Nguyen: Exactly. We often recommend salted hashing with KMS-managed salt rotation. But note salts need to be handled carefully — if you rotate them you lose old mapping unless you store crosswalks.
[04:12] Dr. Lina Ortiz: About retention windows: for this POC what are typical default retention policies?
[04:18] Carlos Nguyen: Hosted defaults could be 30 days for telemetry, but for POC and sensitive flows you can opt-in to ephemeral only with 0-day prompt retention; audit metadata (non-PII) can be kept for 90 days or pushed to your external logs. For Private deployments retention is fully configurable by you.
[04:35] Jared Kim: We want ephemeral prompt retention for PHI flows and a separate telemetry path with minimal fields (no payload) for SLOs. Also we want to validate that request/response bodies are not written to disk or S3 during the flow.
[04:46] Carlos Nguyen: We'll show the runtime architecture during the setup — in short, the inference plane keeps KV cache in memory and we can disable prefix caching persistence, and we can route logs to your S3 with client-side encryption if needed.
[04:57] Maya Patel: Let's map this to success criteria so we can measure pass/fail for the POC. I'll propose:
[05:02] Maya Patel: 1) Security: No raw PHI in persisted logs for the flagged flows, verified by automated scans;
[05:08] Maya Patel: 2) Redaction correctness: >99% recall/precision on synthetic PHI test set;
[05:13] Maya Patel: 3) Performance: p95 latency <350ms on <512 tokens at 120 rps steady and maintain bounded error under spikes to 300 rps;
[05:20] Maya Patel: 4) Operability: KMS integration validated and audit events emitted to customer SIEM;
[05:26] Maya Patel: 5) Cost sensitivity: demonstrable per-token cost estimate within agreed threshold.
[05:31] Jared Kim: Those look good, add that any devtools and benchmark harness must be reproducible and open for our engineers to run locally.
[05:38] Carlos Nguyen: We'll hand over the harness — it's a few python scripts + a JMeter/locust config we use.
[05:45] Maya Patel: Timeline suggestion: Week 0 (this week) finalize scope and data; Week 1 run baseline benchmarks and redaction tests; Week 2 tuning and KMS integration; Week 3 validation and results review. Total ~3 weeks.
[05:58] Samir Desai: We prefer the POC to start 2027-09-13, that gives us time to sanitize and produce the sample sets.
[06:05] Maya Patel: Works for us.
[06:08] Carlos Nguyen: A few technical caveats: if you choose full private deployment you'll need a small infra lead time — we can spin up a dedicated test pool in our hosted sandbox for the benchmark within 48–72 hours if you want faster starts.
[06:21] Aisha Rahman: For the benchmark harness, does the test pool emulate our future production instance, like same GPU types?
[06:27] Carlos Nguyen: We can match GPU class (A100 vs H100) but exact instance sizing will be representative not identical. We'll provide normalized metrics so you can compare.
[06:35] Dr. Lina Ortiz: Can you show us an example of the audit record? We need to check fields.
[06:40] Carlos Nguyen: Sure. Example: {timestamp, request_id, redaction_rules_applied:[rule-id], checksum:sha256(...), model_variant, latency_ms}. We avoid including source text.
[06:50] Jared Kim: checksum must be irreversible and not carry PII, correct?
[06:53] Carlos Nguyen: Correct.
[06:55] Maya Patel: Quick note on metrics: we'll include token counts, model flops, cost-per-token estimate, and p95/p99 latencies in the final bench report.
[07:03] Aisha Rahman: For the synthetic PHI dataset — can Redwood generate it? We don't want to expose even masked production samples.
[07:09] Carlos Nguyen: We can synthesize clinical-like data and insert controlled PHI tokens for redaction tests. But it's ideal if you can produce a representative redacted sample so we test at real distribution.
[07:20] Dr. Lina Ortiz: Ok we will provide a redacted sample and also allow Redwood to generate synthetic stress data.
[07:26] Maya Patel: Anything else on scope?
[07:28] Jared Kim: One more: regression testing for hallucinations. We want to ensure redaction doesn't increase hallucination rates on summaries.
[07:35] Carlos Nguyen: We'll add a quality check: run an eval set comparing outputs with and without redaction preprocessing to measure any delta in ROUGE/BLEU or custom clinical metrics.
[07:46] Samir Desai: Ops question: what logs will go to our SIEM? Only audit events? Or also runtime traces?
[07:52] Carlos Nguyen: That's configurable. For the POC we'll push audit events + sampling of traces (no payload) to your SIEM.
[07:59] Maya Patel: Alright let's recap action items and owner + dates. Carlos will share the benchmark harness, Aisha will provide sanitized sample, Maya will send engagement doc and pricing, Jared will send redaction rules. We'll target start week of 9/13 and have a mid-POC sync end of week 2.
[08:16] Dr. Lina Ortiz: Thanks, that sounds like a plan.
[08:19] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the links and the runbook.
[08:23] Jared Kim: One last thing — can you also include an explicit no-persist guarantee in the POC SOW for the flagged flows?
[08:29] Maya Patel: We'll include a paragraph in the SOW that flags ephemeral only flows and scope.
[08:33] Carlos Nguyen: I'll also attach our KMS integration checklist and the regex/JSON path examples.
[08:38] Aisha Rahman: Great, appreciate it.
[08:40] Maya Patel: End of call, thanks all.

Notes about transcription: some terms may be mis-captured (K V cash for KV cache, etc.), punctuation is rough.
